text: 259 Aletheia is a large main-belt asteroid discovered by German–American astronomer Christian Peters on June 28, 1886, at Litchfield Observatory in Clinton, New York. Classified as an X-type (Tholen: CP-type) asteroid, it is dark and composed of heterogeneous materials containing primitive carbonaceous substances, which account for its low albedo of 0.04. The asteroid has a diameter of approximately 185 kilometers and is among the largest in the main asteroid belt. Its orbit has a semi-major axis of 3.1 AU, an inclination of 11 degrees, and a period of 5.55 years. In 2003, Richard P. Binzel and Schelte Bus contributed to the understanding of Aletheia through the Small Main-belt Asteroid Spectroscopic Survey, Phase II (SMASSII), a lightwave survey that collected visible-wavelength (0.435–0.925 micrometre) spectral data between August 1993 and March 1999. Lightcurve observations have also been conducted by astronomers at the Antelope Hill Observatory, which is officially recognized by the Minor Planet Center. The asteroid is named after Aletheia, the Greek goddess of truth, who is the daughter of Zeus and one of the nurses of Apollo.
